### Analysis

The paper presents a highly significant contribution to the field of instruction-driven image editing. Its core insight—inverting the object removal task to generate training data for object addition using real images rather than synthetic ones—is both clever and robust. The creation of the PIPE dataset (~1M pairs) addresses a critical gap in the literature, as it is the only dataset of its kind to maintain real target images with natural consistency.

The empirical results are impressive. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple independent benchmarks (MagicBrush, OPA) and is substantively validated by a large-scale human study where it was preferred over baselines (InstructPix2Pix) ~72.5% of the time. The data quality is assured by a complex, well-documented filtering pipeline, and the authors show that this dataset can improve general editing capabilities when combined with other data sources.

There are, however, notable weaknesses regarding the evaluation strategy and methodological validation. The most critical issue is the evaluation on the internal PIPE test set. Because this set is generated via the same inversion pipeline as the training data, the metric improvements on this set (e.g., L1 score) are inflated and reflect the model's ability to "undo" the specific artifacts of the dataset generation rather than pure creative addition. The authors correctly identify that the *real* generalization is proved by the independent benchmarks and human evaluation, where the model still wins decisively, though the margin is smaller. While the authors do not appear to make false claims here (they report the numbers and the human preference is the clincher), the presentation requires careful framing to avoid overstating the on-distribution performance.

Other weaknesses include a lack of ablation studies for the extensive filtering pipeline (leaving the necessity of each step speculative), missing analysis of the instruction generation strategies, and a lack of concrete failure case visualizations. These are methodological gaps that would significantly strengthen a paper of this caliber but do not fundamentally invalidate the core contribution.

Overall, the paper is strong, novel, and practical. It offers a new dataset that will likely become a standard resource for the community and a model that outperforms existing methods in both metrics and human perception. The flaws are in the details of the experimental presentation and depth of analysis, not in the core idea or overall validity. Compared to the "Reject/Borderline" thresholds which usually imply a flaw in the idea or insufficient results, this paper clearly surpasses those with its SOTA results and unique data contribution. The flaws keep it from a perfect "Strong Accept" but warrant an entry in the high "Accept" range or the top of the "Accept/Strong Accept" boundary. Given the significant utility of the dataset and the clear SOTA performance on independent grounds, a high score is justified.
